output.summary: Plausible doesn't need awareness. It needs more paying subscribers from a fixed $500/month ad budget, and that budget alone will barely move a base of over 21,000 paying subscribers. The plan pulls three levers. First, find and fix the leak between trial start and paid. Activation is the working hypothesis, confirmed or rejected by the end of week 2. Second, the primary acquisition engine is high-intent 'switching from GA4' and 'analytics without a cookie banner' pages, plus visibility in AI answers. Third, the secondary channel is a tightly scoped Google Search campaign on switcher intent: one big-swing angle test, judged on cost per trial start against a kill line. Channels were ranked with a modified ICE score plus two gates, whether the channel can hit the affordable acquisition cost and how fast it gives a signal. Switcher pages scored 64 of 125 and Search ads 24. Everything else is on the not-doing list with a reason, including a decision not to start a new founder-led LinkedIn programme. Measurement stays cookieless and on-brand: UTMs, Plausible's own goals, billing cohorts and a 'how did you hear about us?' question, with no Google tag on the site. Plan prices, margin, trial volume and conversion rates are not in the confirmed facts. Plan prices are copied on day 1 and the rest is pulled from billing and the product database in week 1. Every target is reset from that baseline. The decision point is the end of week 6: keep, retune or cut ads, and adopt or revert the onboarding change. If no paid channel can clear the affordable acquisition cost, the fallback is an offer change at trial end (annual billing, a stats recap), not more channels. Resources: $500/month ad spend and about 5.5 of an assumed 6 hours a week.
output.positioning: Plausible is the simple, privacy-friendly alternative to Google Analytics. It gives clear numbers on one page with no cookies and no personal data, so there is no cookie banner or GDPR consent form to run. The script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics, so the site stays fast. Proof: over 21,000 paying subscribers and over 313 billion pageviews tracked. Trust: independent, self-funded, profitable, EU-based, and it does not sell customer data. Four angles carry this position into every channel: (1) no cookie banner or consent form, (2) one-page simplicity, (3) a tiny script and a fast site, (4) independent EU ownership and no data selling. Grounding status: no voice-of-customer bank was provided, so today these angles rest on confirmed facts and on Plausible's own site copy ('no training needed', 'Google Analytics is overkill for most site owners'), not on customer words. Week-1 task: tag third-party reviews, free-text signup answers, and recent support and cancellation messages by angle. Record each verbatim quote with its source and count mentions per angle [NEEDS FACT: customer verbatims and counts per angle]. The angle customers raise more often leads ad and page headlines. If the counts contradict the order above, the counts win. Copy says what the product does (no cookies, no personal data). It never promises a legal compliance outcome.

experiments.name: Search ads big swing: privacy package vs simplicity package
experiments.hypothesis: Switchers respond more to 'no cookie banner or consent form' (ad plus matching privacy page) than to 'one-page simplicity' (ad plus GA4 comparison page). The two packages differ in angle and destination at once, so the swing is large enough to detect. Evidence: both are confirmed product facts, and they match the two high-confidence audiences in the insights. Decisions informed: (1) keep or cut ads, (2) which angle leads switcher page headlines from week 7.
experiments.population: Google Search users matching the switcher keyword set in the chosen markets, split 50/50 with a Google Ads experiment. Same keywords, bids, schedule and budget in both arms.
experiments.primaryMetric: Trial starts per click by arm, from Plausible UTM data, plus cost per trial start against the kill line. Ad CTR is a secondary early read only. Budget check: six weeks of the $500 monthly budget is about $700, so affordable clicks ≈ $700 ÷ actual CPC. CPC is unknown until week 2; the owner pulls Keyword Planner estimates in week 1. Clicks needed per arm to detect a doubling of the click-to-trial rate ≈ 16 × p × (1 − p) ÷ p², which simplifies to 16 × (1 − p) ÷ p, where p is the baseline click-to-trial rate. Planning example with an assumed p of 10%, to be replaced by week-2 data: about 144 clicks per arm, so roughly 290 clicks in total, which $700 buys only if CPC stays under about $2.40. If affordable clicks fall short of that, the arm comparison is labelled directional before launch.
guardrails: Cost per trial start in each arm at or below the kill line
Under 20% of spend on terms later added as negatives
No change to landing pages, keywords or bids during the test
Total spend at or below $500 per calendar month
experiments.stoppingRule: These are business thresholds, not a significance test, and are set before launch. Decide when each arm reaches the required clicks or at the end of week 6, whichever comes first. Keep or cut ads: if neither arm's cost per trial is at or below the kill line, cut ads, return the budget and move to the offer fallback. Angle: if one arm's trial starts per click are at least 50% higher and it clears the kill line, move all spend to it and use its angle in page headlines. If the gap is under 10%, angle isn't the lever; keep the cheaper arm if it clears the kill line. Anything in between: iterate once with the 'tiny script' vs 'independent EU' pair. The only early stop is a guardrail breach.

experiments.name: Activation onboarding sequence vs current
experiments.hypothesis: Trials that never get data flowing can't see the product's value. A setup-focused day-0/2/5 sequence plus a dashboard empty-state nudge will raise the share of trials with data within 7 days by at least 30% relative. Decision informed: whether the new sequence becomes the default, and whether activation is the real constraint.
experiments.population: All new trial signups during the window, randomly split 50/50 at signup (for example by account ID parity). Existing trials are excluded.
experiments.primaryMetric: Share of trials with first data integration (script detected or GA4 import) within 7 days. Secondary: trial-to-paid, read after the 30-day trial ends. Volume: the insights propose stopping at 200 trial signups per version. With an assumed 50% baseline (replace with week-1 data), detecting a 30% relative lift (an absolute gap of 15 points) needs about 16 × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.15² ≈ 180 per version, so 200 is enough. Run time = 200 ÷ weekly trial starts per version.
guardrails: Unsubscribe rate on onboarding emails no higher than on the current sequence
Spam complaints below Gmail's published bulk-sender limit of 0.3%, aiming for 0.1% or lower (Gmail sender guidelines)
Support tickets per trial no higher than control
experiments.stoppingRule: Decide at 200 trial signups per version or after 4 weeks of enrolment (the insights' rule), whichever comes first. If the week-1 baseline turns out high (most trials already integrate), recompute the volume and accept that activation isn't the main leak. Scale: at least 30% relative lift in 7-day integration with guardrails holding, so the new sequence becomes the default. Kill: under 10%, so revert and treat the trial-end step or acquisition as the constraint. Iterate once: anything between.

experiments.name: Switcher page rebuild: before/after read
experiments.hypothesis: Rebuilding the GA4 comparison and migration pages around one clear trial call to action and confirmed proof raises trial starts from those pages. Decision informed: whether to roll the same template out to the 4 new high-intent pages.
experiments.population: Organic and AI-referred visitors landing on the rebuilt pages. Paid traffic is excluded by UTM so the ads test doesn't contaminate the read.
experiments.primaryMetric: Trial starts per 100 entrances on the rebuilt pages, comparing 4 weeks before with 4 weeks after on the same weekday mix, using Plausible goal conversions by entry page. Directional only: a before/after read is not causal proof.
guardrails: No other change to those pages or the signup flow during the window
Confounds logged: launches, press, seasonality, Google core updates
Exit rate on the page not materially worse
experiments.stoppingRule: Read once, 4 weeks after the change; no peeking and reverting. A rise of 30% or more in trial starts per 100 entrances means applying the template to the new pages. Under 10%, keep the old structure and test a bigger swing (an audience-specific headline). In between, iterate once. Always labelled directional.

output.diagnosis: Named constraint, a hypothesis to confirm by the end of week 2: a conversion leak between trial start and first data. A trial can't show value until the script is installed or GA4 data is imported. Evidence for it: the insights single out First Data Integration within 7 days as the activation metric to improve, and a self-serve, no-card 30-day trial is easy to start and easy to abandon. The evidence is thin, because no trial or activation numbers were provided. Why this comes before acquisition: $500/month in ads against a base of over 21,000 paying subscribers can add only a small number of customers, while an activation leak cuts the value of every trial from every source, organic and referral included. What would prove this wrong: (a) If week-1 data shows that most trials already integrate within 7 days (assumption for the bar: about three in four, set with the owner) and integrated trials convert to paid well, activation isn't the leak. The constraint is demand capture: pages and ads move to the front and activation work shrinks to a weekly check. (b) If integrated trials still don't convert to paid, the problem is perceived value or price at trial end. The next move is the trial-end offer fallback, not more traffic.
output.affordableCac: Subscription formula: affordable cost to acquire a customer = monthly gross profit per new subscriber × payback months. Inputs: monthly revenue per new subscriber = plan prices (copied from the pricing page on day 1) weighted by the plan mix of new subscribers (from billing in week 1). Gross margin is an assumption of 80%, validated by the end of week 1. Payback is 3 months, an assumption taken from the playbook default for SMB-priced SaaS, which the owner confirms or replaces by the end of week 1. So affordable cost = revenue per new subscriber × 0.8 × 3. Ad kill line: maximum cost per trial start = affordable cost × trial-to-paid rate (from billing cohorts in week 1). Both numbers go at the top of the scorecard. Channel check: switcher pages, AI visibility and activation work cost staff time only, so they fit at any price. Google Search ads fit only if measured cost per trial start by the end of week 6 sits at or below the kill line, which is why spend is capped at $500/month. Meta ads, LinkedIn ads and outbound are rejected partly because a low monthly self-serve price is unlikely to carry them; this is rechecked once the real figure exists. If margin comes in below the assumption, the kill line drops in proportion and ads are the first line cut. Offer fallback if no paid channel clears the kill line: don't add channels. Instead test changes that raise value per customer at trial end: (1) prompt trial users to choose annual billing at conversion, which collects more cash up front and raises the affordable cost on a cash basis [NEEDS FACT: whether annual billing and any annual discount exist]; (2) a trial-end email recapping the user's own traffic stats before the trial lapses. No invented discounts, countdowns or scarcity.

phases.name: Foundation
phases.focus: Copy prices on day 1. Pull the baseline: trials, 7-day integration, trial-to-paid, sources, plan mix and margin. phases.name: Test
phases.focus: Run the activation split and the Search experiment to their pre-registered volumes without peeking or stopping early. Weekly search-term review. phases.name: Commit and compound
phases.focus: Roughly three quarters of effort on the primary: the remaining high-intent pages with the winning angle in headlines, the AI-answer consistency pass and genuine community answers. posts.title: Analytics script size and site speed
posts.body:
Our analytics script is 54 times smaller than Google Analytics. Your visitors never see either one, but their browsers download it on every visit.

That's the odd thing about analytics. It has no button, no image and no layout shift, so it rarely gets looked at the way a hero photo does. It still has to be fetched and run before some visitors have read your headline. A smaller script means less for the browser to do.

You can check this on your own site in a couple of minutes. Open your browser's developer tools, go to the Network tab, reload the page and sort by size. Find the analytics script and compare it with your images, fonts and other scripts. If it outweighs things your visitors actually look at, it's the first place to trim.

Three questions to ask any vendor whose script runs on every page of your site: who pays you, who owns you, and do you sell the data?

An analytics script sees every visit to every page. So the vendor's business model matters as much as its feature list. A free tool has to be paid for somehow, and a company owned by investors answers to them first. The answers tell you whose interests the tool serves when they differ from yours.

Here are ours. Over 21,000 paying subscribers fund Plausible, and they've had over 313 billion pageviews tracked through it. We're independently operated, self-funded and profitable, and we're based in the EU. We don't sell customer data.

You can ask these questions of any tool, ours included. Put them in writing, and notice which vendors answer plainly and which ones change the subject.

**Pre-committed budget rule:**

experiments.name: Headline lab: rotated angles on shared Google Search keywords, single neutral landing page
experiments.hypothesis: Formkit's three differentiators will pull searchers differently: the Google Forms gaps, no cut on payments, and building inside Claude or ChatGPT. The evidence for each is in the confirmed facts and on Formkit's own compare table. At least one angle will beat the others on CTR by a margin worth acting on, without bringing in lower-quality sign-ups. The winner becomes the lead headline on the homepage, pages and upgrade prompts.
experiments.population: Searchers on the shared exact- and phrase-match keyword set, in the countries Formkit sells to (founder confirms in week 1). Each search is served one of the angle ads, rotated evenly within the same ad groups. Keywords, schedule, geography and bids are the same for every angle. All clicks land on the same neutral page, which is not changed during the test.
experiments.primaryMetric: CTR per angle. Secondary decision read: activated sign-ups ÷ clicks per angle. Cost read: cost per activated sign-up.
guardrails: Total test spend capped at $600
Cost per activated sign-up compared with the ceiling in the affordable CAC section; a miss blocks scaling
Impression balance: if one angle gets less than half the impressions of another despite even rotation, report the result as a selection, not a test
Junk or spam sign-ups stay a small minority of ad sign-ups (founder spot-check each week)
experiments.stoppingRule:
**Volume:** clicks needed per angle are computed in week 2 with the standard two-variant approximation, using the Keyword Planner CTR estimate. Run three angles if the $600 cap covers that volume. Otherwise run two angles, or label the test directional.

**Timing:** minimum two weeks, maximum four. Decide at the computed volume or at the end of week 6, whichever comes first. No early stop except a guardrail breach.

**Scale:** the best angle's CTR is at least a quarter higher than each other angle, its activated-sign-up rate per click is no lower than theirs, and the cost ceiling holds. The angle becomes the site and prompt headline, and ads continue on it up to $600 a month.

**Headline-only win:** CTR wins but the cost ceiling is missed. The angle still becomes the headline, and ads stop.

**Kill:** CTR differences under a tenth. Stop ads, leave the budget unspent and move the hours to pages.

**In between:** rewrite the weakest angle using the voice-of-customer phrases with the highest counts, and run one more two-week round capped at half the monthly budget.

These are business thresholds, not significance tests.

output.diagnosis:
**Constraint:** free users are not becoming paying customers. A free plan that removes most reasons to pay makes this worse.

**Evidence:**
- The free plan includes unlimited forms, responses and members (confirmed).
- The features that justify Pro (payments, own domain, badge removal, AI replies, quizzes) sit behind a $6 paywall that many free users may never reach (site insights).
- At $6 a seat, a paid channel only works if free-to-paid is strong. The allowable cost per free sign-up is the affordable CAC times the free-to-paid rate, which is very small at plausible rates.
- More traffic without a better upgrade path mostly adds free users, and adds AI cost with them.
- The lack of reviews and customer names (site insights) also weakens trust at the upgrade moment. That is why review collection and customer-language capture sit inside the plan.

**What would prove this wrong:** week-1 data shows a free-to-paid rate the founder judges healthy and a high upgrade rate among users who hit a Pro feature, while sign-ups are low or flat. Then the real constraint is demand capture: switcher pages and AI visibility become primary, and the upgrade path drops to hygiene.
output.affordableCac:
**Method:** subscription formula with a payback target under three months, the plan's default for SMB-priced SaaS.
- Monthly billing: affordable CAC per seat = monthly price × gross margin × 3 months.
- Yearly billing: price × 10 paid months (two months free) × gross margin, collected up front.

**Per plan:**

| Plan and billing | Affordable CAC per seat |
|---|---|
| Pro monthly | $6 × 3 × margin |
| Pro yearly | $6 × 10 × margin |
| Business monthly | $19 × 3 × margin |
| Business yearly | $19 × 10 × margin |

**Inputs still needed:**
- [NEEDS FACT: gross margin after AI inference costs, from week-1 data]
- [NEEDS FACT: seats per paying account and plan mix]

Until week-1 data shows a yearly or Business share, the working ceiling per new paying account is the Pro monthly figure. Every shift to yearly billing raises the ceiling for that seat by more than three times (ten paid months up front instead of three).

**Channel check:** maximum cost per free sign-up = affordable CAC × free-to-paid rate [NEEDS FACT: free-to-paid rate]. Suppose every dollar of three months of Pro revenue counted as profit. Even then, a free-to-paid rate in the low single digits (assumption until week 1) puts this ceiling well under a dollar per free sign-up.

Paid search will very likely miss that ceiling, so the search test runs as a headline lab and scales only if its pre-set rule is met. The upgrade path, switcher pages, AI visibility and directory listings carry no media cost and fit by construction.

If free-to-paid is still too low at the mid-point review, the fix is packaging (what sits behind Pro, how yearly is presented), not more channels.

Pro costs $6 a seat a month. On payments, Formkit takes nothing: the money goes straight to your own Stripe account.

If you sell through a form, say a deposit for a booking or a paid place at an event, the number that matters isn't the seat price. It's what comes off each payment.

posts.title: Four signs your Google Form has outgrown Google Forms
posts.body:
Google Forms is free and fine for plenty of forms. Here are four signs yours has outgrown it.

Our comparison table lists the gaps: your own link, drop-off by question, kept partial answers and version history. Each one shows up in a different moment.

The link shows up when a client gets your form and sees Google's address, not yours. On Formkit, your own domain is on Pro at $6 a seat a month.

Drop-off by question shows up when half your leads start the form and you can't tell which question they quit on. Kept partial answers matter for the same reason: someone who types their name and email and then leaves is still a person you can follow up with.
